title: The Palantir-based DAR software identifies the author of an emailed amok threat against Siegen's city administration in fractions of a second and 51 of about 100 participants in a Duisburg shooting (28 October 2022)
summary: The North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Ministry said that Palantir-based DAR traced an emailed amok threat in Siegen in fractions of a second and identified 51 of about 100 people at a Duisburg shooting.
account: In October 2022 someone emailed the city administration of Siegen announcing an amok attack. The threat was over the city's “topless” permission for swimming pools. A shooting in Duisburg-Hamborn between a Turkish-Arab clan and the Hells Angels injured four people. Interior Minister Herbert Reul addressed the Landtag's interior committee on 27 October. He said that DAR, the police's Palantir software, links the weapons register, residents' registration, the police case system and the wanted-persons portal. On 28 October 2022 the Interior Ministry of North Rhine-Westphalia said that DAR was central in several recent cases (WELT; RP Online). The ministry said that the email address revealed the suspect via Palantir in fractions of a second. A Duisburg investigator said that police quickly identified 51 of the roughly 100 participants in the shooting, at about 20 minutes each (RP Online; WELT). Of these, 49 were assigned to rival groups. The ministry puts the 2019–2025 cost at about 39 million euros. The opposition attacks the software on data-protection and cost grounds (WELT). In October 2022 the civil-rights group Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (GFF) filed a constitutional complaint against the state police law that allowed this data analysis. North Rhine-Westphalia rewrote the legal basis at the end of 2025. In February 2026 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to decide the complaint and ordered the state to pay the complainants' costs (GFF).
purpose: DAR was procured to let North Rhine-Westphalia police search and link entries across police and administrative databases during investigations. Identifying suspects from an email address or from a nickname and phone number was that purpose.
system: DAR (Datenbankübergreifende Recherche und Analyse), Palantir software used by North Rhine-Westphalia police
deployer: North Rhine-Westphalia police, under the NRW Ministry of the Interior (contract since 2019)

ratings.reason: NRW police resolved an amok-threat email address to a person in fractions of a second. They identified 51 of about 100 shooting participants at about 20 minutes each, per the ministry and a Duisburg investigator. No comparison with conventional methods and no charges or convictions are reported.

Siegen's administration and public had the author of a threatened amok attack identified. The sources do not say whether the threat was credible, whether the person was charged, or what harm was averted.

ai_role.statement: The reports describe DAR as software that links entries across the weapons register, residents' registration data, the police case system and the wanted-persons portal. None mentions machine learning. The minister himself describes plain linking, while the OECD AI Incidents Monitor calls it an AI system. On the ministry's account the software's contribution was speed of identification. That was an email address in fractions of a second and about 20 minutes per shooting participant. Whether manual queries would have reached the same people more slowly is not addressed. The claims come from the deploying ministry and an unnamed investigator.

display.answer: The Siegen and Duisburg results come from the Interior Ministry of North Rhine-Westphalia and a Duisburg investigator, as relayed by WELT and RP Online on 28 October 2022. The Westfalenpost reports the Siegen threat itself. The page of the civil-rights group GFF, which brought the constitutional complaint, covers only the later litigation. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor entry describes the same two cases.
The geopolitical implications are unclear.

fields.summary: The North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Ministry said that Palantir-based DAR traced an emailed amok threat in Siegen in fractions of a second and identified 51 of about 100 people at a Duisburg shooting.
fields.account: In October 2022 someone emailed the city administration of Siegen announcing an amok attack. The threat was over the city's “topless” permission for swimming pools. A shooting in Duisburg-Hamborn between a Turkish-Arab clan and the Hells Angels injured four people. Interior Minister Herbert Reul addressed the Landtag's interior committee on 27 October. He said that DAR, the police's Palantir software, links the weapons register, residents' registration, the police case system and the wanted-persons portal. On 28 October 2022 the Interior Ministry of North Rhine-Westphalia said that DAR was central in several recent cases (WELT; RP Online). The ministry said that the email address revealed the suspect via Palantir in fractions of a second. A Duisburg investigator said that police quickly identified 51 of the roughly 100 participants in the shooting, at about 20 minutes each (RP Online; WELT). Of these, 49 were assigned to rival groups. The ministry puts the 2019–2025 cost at about 39 million euros. The opposition attacks the software on data-protection and cost grounds (WELT). In October 2022 the civil-rights group Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte (GFF) filed a constitutional complaint against the state police law that allowed this data analysis. North Rhine-Westphalia rewrote the legal basis at the end of 2025. In February 2026 the Federal Constitutional Court declined to decide the complaint and ordered the state to pay the complainants' costs (GFF).
